hospice_refusal: A competent adult may give instructions to provide, withhold, or withdraw health care, including life-sustaining treatment, under the Uniform Health-Care Decisions Act (NMSA 1978, Chapter 24, Article 7A). Hospice care focuses on comfort and symptom relief rather than treatment to prolong life.
maid_eligibility: An adult age 18 or older who is a New Mexico resident, has a terminal illness with a prognosis of six months or less, is capable of making health care decisions, is acting voluntarily, and is able to self-administer the medication.
maid_safeguards: The patient must complete the written Request for Medication to End My Life in a Peaceful Manner form witnessed by two people, and the prescription may not be filled until 48 hours after it is written. Only the patient may make the request, not a family member, proxy, or advance directive, and only the patient may self-administer the medication.
notes: The State Bar's Modest Means Helpline phone (505-797-6013) is from the State Bar of New Mexico; the general Lawyer Referral Service is listed on the Bar's directory page. Witness rules for the advance directive form were not verified from an official source, so that field is null.
polst_name: MOST (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: A MOST is a medical order signed by a physician, advanced practice nurse, or physician assistant and by the patient or health care decision maker. It covers resuscitation, medical interventions, and artificial nutrition and hydration, and emergency personnel follow it.
proxy_how: Name an agent in Part 1 of the Optional Advance Health-Care Directive. The agent makes health care decisions for you when you are unable to make them yourself, following your instructions in the directive.
proxy_name: Agent under a Power of Attorney for Health Care

advance_directive_name: Health Care Proxy form and Living Will
advance_directive_requirements: The Health Care Proxy must be signed in front of two witnesses. New York has no statute governing living wills; a living will is recognized under case law (In re Westchester County Medical Center, 72 N.Y.2d 517 (1988)).
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may refuse treatment, including life-sustaining treatment. If a patient lacks capacity and has no health care agent, the Family Health Care Decisions Act allows a surrogate from a listed priority order to make decisions.
maid_eligibility: An adult age 18 or older who is a New York resident, has a terminal illness or condition expected to cause death within six months, and has decision-making capacity.
maid_law: Medical Aid in Dying Act, S.138/A.136, Public Health Law Article 28-F, signed February 6, 2026, effective August 5, 2026
maid_safeguards: The patient must make an oral request recorded by audio or video and submit a written request to the attending physician, and two physicians must confirm the diagnosis. A mental health evaluation is required, the request may only be made by the patient (not by a health care agent or through an advance directive), and only the patient may self-administer the medication; lethal injection and lethal infusion do not qualify.
notes: This is a new law: signed February 6, 2026 and effective August 5, 2026, after a six-month period for Department of Health regulations. The governor's newsroom page and the Senate's Public Health Law Article 28-F text confirm the statute.
polst_name: MOLST (Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment), DOH-5003
polst_note: MOLST is a set of medical orders completed by a health care practitioner for a patient with a serious health condition. It covers CPR, intubation, hospitalization, and other life-sustaining treatment, and is the authorized form for a nonhospital do-not-resuscitate and do-not-intubate order.
proxy_how: Name an adult agent in the Health Care Proxy form, with an alternate if you wish. The agent makes any and all health care decisions for you when your doctor determines you cannot make them yourself, including decisions about life-sustaining treatment, and must follow your known wishes, including about artificial nutrition and hydration.
proxy_name: Health care agent under a Health Care Proxy (Public Health Law Article 29-C)

advance_directive_name: Advance Directive for a Natural Death (living will) and Health Care Power of Attorney
advance_directive_requirements: Both documents must be signed in front of two qualified witnesses. The Health Care Power of Attorney must also be proved by a notary public, and the living will must be proved by a notary public or a clerk of superior court.
hospice_refusal: Under N.C.G.S. 90-321, a person may declare a desire for a natural death, directing that life-prolonging measures be withheld or withdrawn in a terminal condition or persistent vegetative state. Hospice care provides comfort care for a terminal illness.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in North Carolina; no statute authorizes a physician to prescribe medication for that purpose.
notes: The Secretary of State runs an optional Advance Health Care Directive Registry ($10 filing fee). A 2025 bill (H349) proposed updating health care power of attorney and advance directive requirements; the signing rules stated here are the current statutory rules as described in the legislature's bill text and the Secretary of State's materials.
polst_name: MOST (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: A MOST, authorized by N.C.G.S. 90-21.17, is a physician's order that travels with you, including in an ambulance. It must be signed by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner and by the patient or the patient's representative, and it covers CPR, intubation, antibiotics, IV fluids, and hospitalization.
proxy_how: Name an agent in the statutory Health Care Power of Attorney form. The agent has broad power to make health care decisions for you when you cannot make or communicate them yourself, including decisions about life-sustaining treatment.
proxy_name: Health care agent under a Health Care Power of Attorney (N.C.G.S. 32A-25.1)

advance_directive_name: Health Care Directive (N.D.C.C. Chapter 23-06.5; optional form at 23-06.5-17)
advance_directive_requirements: The directive must be in writing, dated, and signed, and the signature must be verified by a notary public or by two witnesses age 18 or older. The agent must also sign to accept the appointment.
hospice_refusal: Every competent adult has the right to make decisions about their own health care, including the decision to have health care provided, withheld, or withdrawn (N.D.C.C. 23-06.5-01). A health care directive lets you state those choices in advance for a period of incapacity.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized. N.D.C.C. 12.1-16-04 makes intentionally aiding, abetting, facilitating, or prescribing a drug or instrument for another person's suicide a Class C felony, and N.D.C.C. 23-06.5-01 states the Health Care Directives chapter does not condone, authorize, or approve mercy killing.
notes: North Dakota uses one combined document for both the agent appointment and treatment instructions, rather than separate living will and power of attorney forms. The 12.1-16-04 penalty text was confirmed from the Century Code chapter as reproduced in search results; the legis.nd.gov chapter 23-06.5 PDF is the official source for the directive.
polst_note: No POLST form is created by North Dakota statute. A clinician can advise on medical orders for a seriously ill patient, but no statewide POLST program was verified.
proxy_how: Name an agent (and an alternate) in Part I of the Health Care Directive. The agent may make any health care decision you could make, subject to limits you write in, and the directive and the agent's authority take effect only when you lack capacity, as certified in writing by your attending physician, psychiatrist, or psychologist.

advance_directive_name: Living Will Declaration (Ohio Rev. Code Chapter 2133) and Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care (Ohio Rev. Code 1337.11-1337.17)
advance_directive_requirements: Each document is valid only if acknowledged before a notary public or signed by at least two adult witnesses present when you sign or who acknowledge your signature.
hospice_refusal: A Living Will Declaration records decisions about life-sustaining treatment you do or do not want if you cannot make decisions yourself. Ohio law expressly preserves the withholding or withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment and comfort care under the living will and DNR laws.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized. Ohio Rev. Code 3795.02 declares assisting suicide against the public policy of the state, and 3795.04 makes knowingly causing another person to commit or attempt suicide by providing the means or participating in the act a felony of the third degree.
notes: No single state-agency advance directive form URL was verified from an official source, so advance_directive_url is null; the forms are in the Ohio Revised Code chapters cited. No referral-service phone was verified on an official page, so help_phone is null.
polst_note: Ohio has not adopted a statewide POLST form. Ohio instead uses a Do Not Resuscitate Comfort Care order (DNRCC or DNRCC-Arrest), a medical order signed by a doctor, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant.
proxy_how: Name an attorney in fact in the Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care. The agent's authority takes effect only when your doctor determines you have lost the capacity to make informed health care decisions, and the agent ensures your wishes about life-sustaining treatment are carried out.
proxy_name: Attorney in fact (health care agent) under a Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care

advance_directive_name: Advance Directive for Health Care (Oklahoma Advance Directive Act, 63 O.S. 3101.1-3101.16)
hospice_refusal: The Oklahoma Advance Directive Act recognizes the right of individuals to control aspects of their own medical care, including the right to decline medical treatment or direct that it be withdrawn, even if death ensues (63 O.S. 3101.2).
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized. The Oklahoma Advance Directive Act (63 O.S. 3101.2) states it does not condone, authorize, or approve mercy killing, assisted suicide, or euthanasia, and aiding suicide is addressed in 21 O.S. 813-814.
notes: No Oklahoma POST/POLST program and no advance directive signing rule were verified from an official source, so those fields are null. The advance directive URL is the Oklahoma Health Care Authority SoonerCare handbook (official state publication) describing living wills and the toll-free number to request the form; the 800-522-8065 number is the Oklahoma Bar Association toll-free number shown on okbar.org. No bar referral page URL was verified, so help_url is null.
proxy_how: Name a health care proxy in the Advance Directive for Health Care. For a qualified patient, the proxy, in consultation with the attending physician, has authority to make treatment decisions, including providing, withholding, or withdrawing life-sustaining procedures.

advance_directive_name: Oregon Advance Directive for Health Care (OHA 3905)
advance_directive_requirements: You must sign the form, and it must be witnessed by two witnesses or a notary.
hospice_refusal: An advance directive lets you write down treatments you do or do not want, such as a breathing machine or feeding tube, before you need them. You may refuse or withdraw life-sustaining treatment, and a POLST turns those wishes into medical orders.
maid_eligibility: An adult age 18 or older who is capable of making and communicating health care decisions and has a terminal illness expected to cause death within six months. The residency requirement was repealed in 2023 (HB 2279).
maid_law: Oregon Death with Dignity Act, ORS 127.800-127.897
maid_safeguards: The patient must make two oral requests at least 15 days apart and one written request signed and dated in the presence of two witnesses. An attending physician and a consulting physician must confirm the diagnosis and capacity, the patient may rescind the request at any time, and only the patient may self-administer the medication. Lethal injection, mercy killing, and euthanasia are prohibited.
notes: The 15-day waiting period may be waived for a patient whose death is imminent under the 2019 amendments. The Oregon Health Authority FAQ confirms the POLST registry URL and that POLST forms come from the patient's physician.
polst_note: A POLST is a medical order signed by a physician, naturopathic physician, nurse practitioner, or physician associate, and it is filed in the statewide Oregon POLST Registry (ORS 127.663-127.684). It records wishes for emergency treatment, including resuscitation, and is for seriously ill patients rather than healthy adults.
proxy_how: Name a health care representative in the Advance Directive form. The representative makes health care decisions for you if you become too sick to speak for yourself or are unable to make your own medical decisions. If you have no effective appointment, a representative is appointed for you in the priority order in ORS 127.635.

advance_directive_name: Advance Health Care Directive (combined Living Will and Durable Health Care Power of Attorney), Act 169 of 2006, 20 Pa.C.S. Chapter 54
advance_directive_requirements: The directive must be dated and signed by the principal and two adult witnesses. Notarization is not required in Pennsylvania, but is recommended.
hospice_refusal: A living will takes effect when your attending physician determines you lack the ability to understand, make, or communicate health care decisions and you are permanently unconscious or have an end-stage medical condition. You may refuse or withdraw life-sustaining treatment under the Advance Directive for Health Care Act.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized. Under 18 Pa.C.S. 2505, a person who intentionally aids or solicits another to die by suicide is guilty of a felony of the second degree if the conduct causes a suicide or attempted suicide, and otherwise of a misdemeanor of the second degree. Bills to authorize it (HB 1109 / SB 570, 2025) had not passed as of 2026.
notes: The POLST URL is the PA POLST program's official guidance document; the form itself is available through papolst.org. The PBA Lawyer Referral Service covers 47 of 67 counties; other counties use local bar referral services.
polst_name: PA POLST (Pennsylvania Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: PA POLST is a medical order, not an advance directive, for people with serious illness. It is completed by a doctor, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner with the patient, printed on pink card stock, and translates wishes into orders for CPR, medical interventions, and other treatment.
proxy_how: Appoint an agent in the Durable Health Care Power of Attorney part of the Advance Health Care Directive. The agent makes health and personal care decisions for you when you are unable to do so, including decisions about life-sustaining treatment, artificial nutrition and hydration, and organ donation.
proxy_name: Health care agent under a Durable Health Care Power of Attorney

advance_directive_name: Living Will Declaration (Rights of the Terminally Ill Act, R.I. Gen. Laws Chapter 23-4.11) and Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care (Chapter 23-4.10)
advance_directive_requirements: The Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care must be signed by one notary public or two qualified witnesses present when you sign or acknowledge your signature. The living will declaration must be signed in the presence of two subscribing witnesses who are not related to you by blood or marriage.
hospice_refusal: The Rights of the Terminally Ill Act allows a person to instruct physicians to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining procedures in a terminal condition. A competent adult may refuse treatment, and hospice care provides comfort care for a terminal illness.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Rhode Island; no statute authorizes a physician to prescribe medication for that purpose.
notes: Rhode Island does not use the terms health care proxy or health care representative in its statutes; the decision maker is the agent under the durable power of attorney. No specific assisted-suicide prohibition statute was verified from an official source, so that cite is omitted rather than guessed.
polst_note: MOLST, under R.I. Gen. Laws Chapter 23-4.11, is a voluntary medical order signed by the patient or health care decision maker and a physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant. It directs providers on resuscitation and life-sustaining measures and travels with the patient between facilities.
proxy_how: Name one agent in the Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care form. The agent may make any health care decision you could make yourself when your doctor determines you are unable to communicate health care decisions, and no terminal condition is needed for the power to take effect.
proxy_name: Agent (attorney in fact) under a Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care

advance_directive_name: Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death (living will, S.C. Code Title 44, Chapter 77) and Health Care Power of Attorney (S.C. Code 62-5-501 to 62-5-518)
advance_directive_requirements: The Health Care Power of Attorney must be signed by two witnesses. The Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death must be signed by two witnesses and an officer authorized to administer oaths.
hospice_refusal: Under S.C. Code 44-77-30, life-sustaining procedures may be withheld or withdrawn when a person age 18 or older has a qualifying declaration and two physicians who personally examined the person certify a terminal condition or permanent unconsciousness. Hospice care provides comfort care for a terminal illness.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized. S.C. Code 16-3-1090 makes it unlawful to assist another person in committing suicide, punishable as a felony by up to 15 years imprisonment or a fine up to $100,000, or both.
notes: South Carolina's living-will statute is titled the Death With Dignity Act (Title 44, Chapter 77), which is a declaration for a natural death, not a medical aid in dying law. The SC Bar page lists the statutory health care power of attorney forms; the POST URL is the official Code chapter text. The statewide toll-free referral number 1-800-868-2284 also appears in state sources, but the SC Bar page itself lists (803) 799-7100, which is used here.
polst_name: POST (Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: POST, under the Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment Act (S.C. Code Title 44, Chapter 80, 2019 Act No. 89), is a uniform set of medical orders signed by a patient's physician for a person with a serious illness or who may be expected to lose capacity within twelve months. It is portable across health care settings and covers resuscitation, medical interventions, and assisted nutrition and hydration.
proxy_how: Name an agent age 18 or older and of sound mind in the statutory Health Care Power of Attorney form (S.C. Code 62-5-504); the agent may not be your doctor or another health care provider treating you, or their employee. The agent has full authority to make health care decisions for you when you cannot, including decisions about life-sustaining treatment, access to medical records, and placement in a health care or nursing facility.
proxy_name: Health care agent under a Health Care Power of Attorney
